qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Define total cost.
items.canonical_answer: The full cost of producing a specified output in a period.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): The full cost of producing a specified output in a period.
objective_titles: Describe total cost

items.prompt: Define average cost.
items.canonical_answer: Total cost per unit of output.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Total cost per unit of output.
objective_titles: Describe average cost

items.prompt: Define fixed cost.
items.canonical_answer: A cost that does not change with output over the relevant short-run range and period.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): A cost that does not change with output over the relevant short-run range and period.
objective_titles: Describe fixed cost

items.prompt: Define variable cost.
items.canonical_answer: A cost that changes with output in the relevant period.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): A cost that changes with output in the relevant period.
objective_titles: Describe variable cost

items.prompt: Define total revenue.
items.canonical_answer: The money received from selling output in a period.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): The money received from selling output in a period.
objective_titles: Describe total revenue

items.prompt: Define average revenue.
items.canonical_answer: Total revenue per unit sold.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Total revenue per unit sold.
objective_titles: Describe average revenue

items.prompt: Calculate total cost and average cost from invented fixed cost N$600, total variable cost N$800 and output 200 bars.
items.canonical_answer: Total cost = N$600 + N$800 = N$1,400. Average cost = N$1,400 / 200 = N$7 per bar.
marking_guidance: Formula/substitution (1): add N$600 and N$800. Working/result with units (1): divide N$1,400 by 200, giving N$7 per bar.
objective_titles: Define total, average, fixed and variable costs

items.prompt: Analyse the cost pattern using invented existing-capacity output/cost data: 100 bars total cost N$1,000; 200 bars N$1,400. Fixed cost stays N$600.
items.canonical_answer: Total cost rises N$400 while average cost falls N$10 to N$7 per bar. Fixed cost per bar falls N$6 to N$3, explaining the lower average despite a higher total.
marking_guidance: Pattern (1): total up, average down. Evidence/comparison (1): N$10 versus N$7. Explanation (2): same fixed total (1), spread over more bars (1).
objective_titles: Define total, average, fixed and variable costs

items.prompt: Calculate total and average revenue where an invented firm produces 120 bars and sells 100 at a uniform N$8 each.
items.canonical_answer: Total revenue = price × sales = N$8 × 100 = N$800. Average revenue = N$800 / 100 = N$8 per unit sold.
marking_guidance: Formula/substitution (1): N$8 × 100 sales. Working/units (1): N$800 / 100 = N$8 per unit sold, excluding unsold production.
objective_titles: Define total and average revenue

items.prompt: Analyse revenue measures when invented sales are 100 units at N$8 and 50 units at N$6.
items.canonical_answer: Total revenue is N$800 + N$300 = N$1,100; average revenue is N$1,100 / 150, approximately N$7.33 per unit sold. This is sales-weighted, not the simple N$7 mean of prices.
marking_guidance: Pattern (1): differing price groups. Evidence (1): receipts N$1,100. Explanation (2): divide by all 150 sold (1), weighting reflects quantities (1).
objective_titles: Define total and average revenue

items.prompt: Explain the error in dividing N$800 sales revenue by 120 units produced to find average revenue when only 100 units were sold.
items.canonical_answer: Average revenue uses units sold, so it is N$800 / 100 = N$8 per unit sold. The 20 unsold units are production, not sales in the denominator.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): output produced substituted for sales. Boundary/test (1): divide by 100 sold, giving N$8.
objective_titles: Define total and average revenue

items.prompt: Explain the difference between average and marginal revenue using invented total revenue N$800 at 100 units sold and N$806 at 101.
items.canonical_answer: Average revenue at 101 is N$806 / 101, about N$7.98 per unit sold. Marginal revenue for the extra unit is the change N$806 − N$800 = N$6.
marking_guidance: Confusion/boundary (1): per-unit average differs from additional receipts. Test (1): division versus change in totals gives N$7.98 versus N$6.
objective_titles: Define total and average revenue

items.prompt: Calculate the profit change using invented sales/cost totals for the same period: initially revenue N$800 and total cost N$1,000; afterwards N$1,600 and N$1,400.
items.canonical_answer: Profit = revenue − total cost. Initially it is −N$200, a loss; afterwards N$200 profit. The improvement is N$400.
marking_guidance: Formula/substitution (1): N$800−N$1,000 and N$1,600−N$1,400. Working/units (1): −N$200 to N$200, improvement N$400.
objective_titles: Discuss how costs and revenue might change as output changes

items.prompt: Explain why average cost can fall as output rises within existing capacity when fixed cost is unchanged and variable cost per unit stays N$4.
items.canonical_answer: The unchanged fixed total is spread across more output, lowering average fixed cost. With the variable component unchanged per unit, average total cost falls even though total variable cost and total cost rise.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): more output within capacity. Mechanism (2): fixed total unchanged (1), fixed amount per unit falls (1). Consequence (1): average total falls with constant unit variable cost.
objective_titles: Discuss how costs and revenue might change as output changes

items.prompt: Analyse the claim that higher output guarantees higher revenue: invented sales rise from 100 units at N$10 to 150 at N$6.
items.canonical_answer: Sales volume rises but total revenue falls from N$1,000 to N$900. The lower price more than offsets extra sales, so output/sales growth alone does not establish receipts growth.
marking_guidance: Pattern (1): quantity up, receipts down. Evidence (1): N$1,000 versus N$900. Explanation (2): price falls (1), offsets volume increase (1).
objective_titles: Discuss how costs and revenue might change as output changes

items.prompt: Explain why technology adding N$400 weekly fixed cost while saving N$2 variable cost per unit may lower total cost at 300 units but raise it at 100; other costs, quality and methods are comparable.
items.canonical_answer: At 100 units the N$200 variable saving is below the N$400 extra fixed cost, so total cost rises N$200. At 300, saving N$600 exceeds the extra commitment, so total cost falls N$200. The advantage depends on output.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): higher fixed/lower variable costs. Mechanism (2): N$200 saving at 100 (1), N$600 at 300 (1). Consequence (1): output-dependent total cost after N$400 commitment.
objective_titles: Explain the effect of changes in technology on production

items.prompt: Explain why lower variable cost per bar alone cannot establish that new technology raises profit.
items.canonical_answer: Added fixed commitments or other relevant costs can offset the saving, and sales revenue may differ. Compare full total costs and actual saleable output before drawing a profit conclusion.
marking_guidance: Context (1): partial variable saving. Reason/conclusion (1): full cost and revenue determine profit.
objective_titles: Explain the effect of changes in technology on production

items.prompt: Define fixed cost (2). Identify the fixed and variable costs where a weekly premises charge stays N$600 regardless of output and materials cost N$4 per bar (2). Explain why total cost can rise while average cost falls when the unchanged fixed total is spread over more bars and variable cost per bar is unchanged (2). Identify total and average revenue for 100 bars sold at a uniform N$8 each (2).
items.canonical_answer: Fixed cost does not vary with output over the relevant short-run range/period. The premises charge is fixed and materials variable. Spreading the fixed total lowers its unit share, allowing average cost to fall despite more variable inputs raising total cost. Revenue is N$800 total and N$8 per unit sold.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): unchanged with output (1), relevant short-run range/period (1). Separate points for identification (2): premises fixed (1), materials variable (1). Explanation (2): fixed cost spread (1), total variable cost can rise while unit average falls (1). Identification (2): N$800 total (1), N$8 average (1). Marks allocation 8.
objective_titles: Describe fixed cost

items.prompt: Invented weekly existing method within 300-bar capacity: fixed cost N$600, variable cost N$4 per comparable bar. All bars sell at a uniform N$8. Compare outputs 100 and 300. New technology has fixed cost N$1,000 and variable cost N$2 per bar, including all relevant costs; quality and sale prices are unchanged. Required training and power are available. Describe three features of existing costs and revenue at 100 bars, each with a distinguishing figure (6). Explain how existing total cost, average cost and revenue change at 300 compared with 100 (7). Discuss whether the new technology is preferable at both outputs (7).
items.canonical_answer: At 100, fixed cost is N$600, total cost N$1,000 and revenue N$800. At 300, total cost rises to N$1,800, average cost falls N$10 to N$6 and revenue rises to N$2,400, with average revenue N$8 unchanged. Fixed-cost spreading explains the unit fall. New technology costs N$1,200 at 100 but N$1,600 at 300, so it is worse at low output and better at high output under the stated sales and cost conditions.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): fixed cost (1), N$600 figure (1); total cost includes variable (1), N$1,000 figure (1); revenue sales receipts (1), N$800 figure (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): total N$1,800 at 300 (1), average N$10 to N$6 (1), fixed total unchanged (1), spread over more bars (1), revenue N$2,400 (1), price remains N$8 average (1), sold quantity determines total receipts (1). Both sides/judgement (7): technology variable saving (1), extra N$400 fixed commitment (1); total N$1,200 at 100 (1), N$1,600 at 300 (1); condition comparable quality/full costs/sales (1); judgement reject at 100 (1), prefer at 300 (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Invented weekly existing method within 300-bar capacity: fixed cost N$600, variable cost N$4 per comparable bar. All bars sell at a uniform N$8. Compare outputs 100 and 300. New technology has fixed cost N$1,000 and variable cost N$2 per bar, including all relevant costs; quality and sale prices are unchanged. Required training and power are available. Evaluate adopting technology in Case 1 with confirmed sales of 300 bars (7). Evaluate it in Case 2 with demand limited to 100 bars (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: new technology saves N$600 variable cost against N$400 extra fixed cost; profit rises N$600 to N$800, supporting adoption with confirmed sales and feasibility. Case 2: N$200 variable saving does not cover the added N$400 commitment; the loss increases N$200 to N$400. Retain the existing method for this comparison at low demand, reconsidering if demand or cost conditions change.
marking_guidance: Case 1 allocation (7): argument for N$600 saving (1), net N$200 advantage (1); argument against fixed commitment (1), sales/operation risk if conditions fail (1); condition confirmed 300 sales and feasibility (1); judgement adopt (1), profit N$800 exceeds N$600 (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for some variable saving (1), N$200 amount (1); argument against extra fixed N$400 (1), larger N$400 loss (1); condition low demand persists (1); judgement retain existing (1), conditional on matched costs and no wider options assessed (1). Total marks 14.
